Issues.Title: TestHost: `IRequestBodyPipeFeature` is added mid-request on first `Request.BodyReader` access, racing with gRPC duplex streaming response writes (intermittent NullReferenceException only under TestServer)
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

`TestServer` (Microsoft.AspNetCore.TestHost) does not provide `IRequestBodyPipeFeature`: `HttpContextBuilder` sets BodyControl / Response / ResponseBody / RequestLifetime / ResponseTrailers / Upgrade (+ Reset for HTTP/2), and `ClientHandler` sets `IHttpRequestFeature.Body`. Kestrel's `HttpProtocol` implements `IRequestBodyPipeFeature` itself.

Under TestServer, the first access to `HttpContext.Request.BodyReader` therefore creates `RequestBodyPipeFeature` lazily and calls `IFeatureCollection.Set`, which bumps `Revision`. If another thread touches `HttpContext.Response` at the same moment, both threads see the revision change and run `Cache = default` in `FeatureReferences.UpdateCached`. A thread can then read back `null` through the `ref cached` it has just assigned, and `DefaultHttpResponse` throws `NullReferenceException`.

In gRPC duplex streaming this happens without any user code touching `HttpContext` concurrently. With MagicOnion StreamingHub, for example, the server sends response headers, then the hub's `OnConnected` queues server-to-client messages, which a background writer flushes to the response. Right after that, the request thread starts reading the request stream for the first time (`HttpContextStreamReader.MoveNext` → `Request.BodyReader`). On TestServer that first read adds the feature while the writer is writing.

In our test suite (WebApplicationFactory + MagicOnion StreamingHub, GitHub Actions `ubuntu-latest` under CPU load), this made about 3 in 100 CI runs fail. The server logged the exception below for the `Connect` call, and the client saw the stream end ("A task was canceled because the client has disposed.").

The same application on Kestrel (production, and our Kestrel-based tests) does not add any feature mid-stream.


### Expected Behavior

TestServer behaves like Kestrel here: `IRequestBodyPipeFeature` is present from the start of the request (for example, set by `HttpContextBuilder` / `ClientHandler` together with the other features), so reading the request body for the first time does not change the feature collection while the response may be written from another thread.


### Steps To Reproduce

I could not make a deterministic TestServer + gRPC repro: the window is a few instructions wide, and 300 local connect-then-call iterations under artificial CPU load did not hit it. The mechanism can be shown with the same feature shape as TestServer (no `IRequestBodyPipeFeature`) and two threads on one `DefaultHttpContext`.

File-based app, `dotnet run race.cs` (and `dotnet run race.cs -- pre` for the workaround):

```csharp
#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Features;

var pre = args.Length > 0 && args[0] == "pre";
var nre = 0; const int N = 200_000;
for (var i = 0; i < N; i++)
{
    var features = new FeatureCollection();
    features.Set<IHttpRequestFeature>(new HttpRequestFeature { Body = new MemoryStream() });
    features.Set<IHttpResponseFeature>(new HttpResponseFeature());
    features.Set<IHttpResponseBodyFeature>(new StreamResponseBodyFeature(Stream.Null));
    var ctx = new DefaultHttpContext(features);
    _ = ctx.Response.Headers; _ = ctx.Response.BodyWriter;               // caches warmed, as after response headers were sent
    if (pre) { _ = ctx.Request.BodyReader; _ = ctx.Response.BodyWriter; } // workaround: create the feature up front
    using var go = new ManualResetEventSlim();
    var writer = Task.Run(() => { go.Wait(); for (var k = 0; k < 50; k++) { _ = ctx.Response.BodyWriter; _ = ctx.Response.Headers; } });
    var reader = Task.Run(() => { go.Wait(); _ = ctx.Request.BodyReader; });
    go.Set();
    try { Task.WaitAll(writer, reader); }
    catch (AggregateException ex) { nre += ex.InnerExceptions.Count(e => e is NullReferenceException); }
}
Console.WriteLine($"pre={pre} NRE={nre} / {N}");
```

Results (Windows x64, SDK 10.0.401):

- `pre=False`: about 100 NREs out of 200,000 iterations. They include the exact `OnCompleted ← RequestBodyPipeFeature.get_Reader` stack below, plus NREs in `get_BodyWriter` / `get_Headers` on the writer thread.
- `pre=True`: 0.

Workaround in our tests: an `IStartupFilter` middleware that runs `_ = context.Request.BodyReader;` at the start of every request, on the request thread. This creates the feature before any concurrent writer exists.


### Exceptions (if any)

Server side, logged by `Grpc.AspNetCore.Server.ServerCallHandler` ("Error when executing service method 'Connect'"):

```
System.NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object.
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.DefaultHttpResponse.OnCompleted(Func`2 callback, Object state)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Features.RequestBodyPipeFeature.get_Reader()
   at Grpc.AspNetCore.Server.Internal.HttpContextStreamReader`1.MoveNext(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at MagicOnion.Internal.MagicOnionAsyncStreamReader`2.MoveNext(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at MagicOnion.Server.Hubs.StreamingHubBase`2.HandleMessageAsync()
   at MagicOnion.Server.Hubs.StreamingHubBase`2.MagicOnion.Server.Internal.IStreamingHubBase.Connect()
   ...
   at Grpc.AspNetCore.Server.Internal.CallHandlers.DuplexStreamingServerCallHandler`3.HandleCallAsyncCore(HttpContext httpContext, HttpContextServerCallContext serverCallContext)
```

Client side: `System.Threading.Tasks.TaskCanceledException: A task was canceled because the client has disposed.` (MagicOnion client, pending hub call).


### .NET Version

10.0.401

### Anything else?

Related: #42040 (null refs when `HttpContext` is accessed concurrently, caused by the `FeatureReferences` cache being cleared after a new feature is set) and #42100 (closed as part of #42040; NRE in `DefaultHttpRequest.BodyReader`).

This report is about a narrower, TestHost-specific trigger, so I'm filing it separately: TestServer adds a feature to the collection in the middle of a request where Kestrel never does. That turns the concurrent request-read / response-write pattern of gRPC duplex streaming (which works on Kestrel) into a race that only happens in integration tests. The fix suggested below is local to TestHost and does not depend on #42040.

- Microsoft.AspNetCore.TestHost / Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing 10.0.14
- Grpc.AspNetCore.Server 2.57.0, Grpc.Net.Client 2.57.0 (via MagicOnion)
- MagicOnion.Server / MagicOnion.Client 7.11.0
- CI: GitHub Actions `ubuntu-latest` (4 vCPU). Locally the failure did not reproduce under TestServer; it shows up only when many test classes run in parallel on CI.
- I understand that `HttpContext` is not thread-safe in general (#42040). The point here is that duplex streaming legitimately reads the request and writes the response on different threads, and on Kestrel this is safe because the feature collection doesn't change mid-stream. TestHost changes the collection mid-stream, so the race appears only in tests. Providing `IRequestBodyPipeFeature` up front in TestHost would remove it.

Issues.Title: Unquarantine TempData cookie persistence test
Issues.Body:
Fixes #70085.

`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETest.Tests.TempDataCookieTest.TempDataPersistWithoutAccessing` was quarantined after intermittent `StaleElementReferenceException` failures at `WebElement.Click()` (5 distinct builds in the issue's deterministic 30-day snapshot).

## Root cause

The test runs with `PageLoadStrategy.None`. Before #70088, it submitted `set-values-not-read` and immediately searched for `redirect-button`, an ID present on both the departing `/tempdata` page and the destination `/tempdata/redirect_without_read` page. Selenium could return the departing page's element while navigation was replacing that document, making the reference stale at click time.

#70088 fixed the causal race by assigning the destination button the unique ID `redirect-without-read-button` and waiting for that destination-only element with `Browser.Exists(...)`. The final TempData persistence assertion remains unchanged. This PR restores the cookie-backed test to the normal suite now that the causal fix is on `main`.

## Validation

- Exact test passed with Chrome 156.0.8078.73 and matching ChromeDriver 156.0.8078.73.
- Repeated the exact fully qualified test 50 times: 50/50 passed.
- The targeted test command rebuilt `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests` and its required product/test assets successfully before execution.
- `git diff --check` passed.

## CI status

All completed non-Components-E2E checks pass, including code check, source-build, platform tests, Helix subsets, quarantined tests, and template tests. Components E2E CoreCLR also passes.

Build Analysis attributes the two failed Components E2E jobs to unrelated existing flakes:

- `VirtualizationTest.VariableHeight_HtmlTable_DoesNotProduceNestedTrElements` failed in Mono client/WebAssembly with an empty rendered collection; Build Analysis reports a 13.68% historical failure rate.
- `ServerRoutingTest.NavigationLock_CanBlockExternalNavigation` failed in Mono server because navigation remained at `/subdir/`; Build Analysis reports a 31.10% historical failure rate.

Neither test or subsystem is changed by this PR. A one-time GitHub check re-request was attempted for both jobs, but the Azure Pipelines integration rejected it with `403 Resource not accessible by integration`; an authorized Azure rerun is required.

After a full repository `npm run build` and targeted E2E rebuild at this exact head, both unrelated failing tests passed locally with Chrome/ChromeDriver 156:

- `VirtualizationTest.VariableHeight_HtmlTable_DoesNotProduceNestedTrElements`: passed.
- `ServerRoutingTest.NavigationLock_CanBlockExternalNavigation`: passed.

## Residual uncertainty

The original race is timing-dependent, so a finite local stress run cannot prove absence of every browser scheduling variant. The selector now cannot match the departing document, directly removing the stale-reference mechanism recorded in #70085.

Issues.Title: SignalR Java client allocates binary values before validating MessagePack lengths
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues.

### Describe the bug

`MessagePackHubProtocol.java` reads a binary value's length prefix and allocates an array of that size before checking whether the message contains the declared number of bytes:

```java
length = unpacker.unpackBinaryHeader();
byte[] binaryValue = new byte[length];
unpacker.readPayload(binaryValue);
```

A small, malformed message can therefore cause an allocation much larger than its actual payload before parsing detects the missing data.

`parseMessages` validates the outer SignalR message length, but that does not validate length prefixes embedded within the MessagePack body. Its final consumed-byte check also occurs after the allocation.

### Expected Behavior

Validate embedded lengths against the bytes remaining in the current SignalR message before allocating length-dependent buffers. Malformed or truncated values should be rejected without allocating their declared size.

### Steps To Reproduce

Construct a SignalR invocation containing a binary argument whose MessagePack length prefix declares substantially more bytes than are present. Set the outer SignalR frame length to match the actual encoded body, and parse it with a binder expecting a `byte[]` argument.

The binary parsing branch allocates `new byte[length]` before `readPayload` discovers that the bytes are missing.

This reproduction is based on source inspection; it has not been executed.

### Exceptions (if any)

The eventual exception depends on the declared length and available memory. No runtime exception output has been collected.

### .NET Version

N/A — SignalR Java client.

### Anything else?

The confirmed allocation site is the `BINARY` branch of `readValue` in [`MessagePackHubProtocol.java`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/src/SignalR/clients/java/signalr/messagepack/src/main/java/com/microsoft/signalr/messagepack/MessagePackHubProtocol.java). Validation should respect the current message's boundary, not include bytes belonging to subsequent messages in the same buffer.

# Stabilize Blazor Web JS initializer tests

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).

- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making.

Make the Blazor Web initializer setup deterministic and validate the WASM asset path.

## Description

`BlazorWebJsInitializersTest` uses the streaming browser context, whose Selenium page-load strategy does not wait for navigation to complete. The test previously wrote `block-webassembly-settings` to session storage after navigating to `/initializers`, racing the page's `Blazor.start()` call:

- If startup read storage first, the test used the normal WebAssembly settings and usually passed without exercising the intended no-options path. The late value could also leak into a later theory row.
- If the test write won, startup received no WebAssembly settings. The server-project initializer callbacks were registered, but `dotnet.js` was requested from `/subdir/_framework/dotnet.js` instead of the test client's `/subdir/WasmMinimal/_framework/dotnet.js`. Historical failures show that wrong-path request intermittently returning `200 text/plain` with no module MIME type, aborting startup before callbacks were recorded.

The fix passes one-shot initializer settings in the target URL, so they are available before startup without cross-row storage state. The server-project `beforeWebStart` initializer supplies the `/WasmMinimal` resource mapping when the caller intentionally omits WebAssembly options. This preserves the original coverage for #54049: the framework-created `options.webAssembly` object is used by initializers before WebAssembly startup.

The modern test now also asserts that the browser loaded `/WasmMinimal/_framework/dotnet.js`, making the failure path deterministic instead of relying on the wrong route to intermittently return an invalid MIME type. The classic test shares the same setup and is unquarantined as part of the same fix. Related existing proposal: #69193.

## Evidence

Without the `beforeWebStart` mapping, the unchanged regression assertion failed all four WebAssembly rows and the captured network log showed `200 text/javascript - /subdir/_framework/dotnet.js`; all four non-WebAssembly controls passed. With the fix:

- E2E project build: succeeded with 0 warnings and 0 errors.
- Combined modern and classic initializer matrices: 16 passed, 0 failed.
- Ten repeated combined runs: 160 passed, 0 failed.

Remaining uncertainty: validation used local Linux with Chrome 156. The historical MIME failure is environment-sensitive, so the draft should remain open until the repository's Linux/Windows Helix coverage confirms the route assertion and initializer behavior.

Issues.Title: CertificateAuthenticationHandler: the Name claim and the X500DistinguishedName claim disagree about the subject
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

I searched the open and closed issues and found nothing on this.

### Describe the bug

`CertificateAuthenticationHandler.CreatePrincipal` builds two claims from the same client
certificate by two different routes, four lines apart, and the two disagree about the subject:

- `ClaimTypes.X500DistinguishedName` comes from `certificate.SubjectName.Name`, which quotes
  attribute values per RFC 4514.
- `ClaimTypes.Name`, which becomes `User.Identity.Name`, comes from
  `certificate.GetNameInfo(X509NameType.SimpleName, false)`, which does not quote and returns
  only one CN when the subject has several.

`src/Security/Authentication/Certificate/src/CertificateAuthenticationHandler.cs`, lines 264-267
and 282-285 on release/10.0.

### Measured

Self-signed certificates produced with openssl, inspected on `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App` 10.0.14:

| subject | `X500DistinguishedName` claim | `ClaimTypes.Name` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/CN=admin/CN=guest` | `CN=guest, CN=admin` | `guest` |
| `/CN=guest, CN=admin` | `CN="guest, CN=admin"` | `guest, CN=admin` |
| `/CN=admin ` (trailing space) | `CN="admin "` | `admin ` |

Two consequences follow:

1. With two CN attributes the DN claim carries both and the Name claim carries one, so an
   application that authorises on the DN claim and one that authorises on `User.Identity.Name`
   reach different conclusions from a single certificate.
2. With a comma inside the CN the DN claim is correctly quoted and the Name claim is raw, so an
   embedded `CN=admin` is no longer distinguishable from a real RDN by anything downstream that
   treats the Name as a distinguished name, logs it, or matches it against a DN pattern.

### Expected behaviour

Either the two claims agree about the subject, or the difference is documented on
`CertificateAuthenticationHandler` so an application does not assume the Name claim is a
quoted or complete representation of the subject.

### Scope, stated plainly

This is not a chain validation bypass. The certificate still has to chain to a CA the server
trusts, so reaching it needs a CA that will issue a certificate with an attacker-influenced CN.
Where that holds, which is common in automated or self-service internal enrolment, the fields
above are attacker-chosen.

There is one in-box consumer of the Name claim that makes an isolation decision:
`src/Mvc/Mvc.TagHelpers/src/Cache/CacheTagKey.cs` line 100 uses `httpContext.User?.Identity?.Name`
as part of the cache key for `<cache vary-by-user>`.

`CreatePrincipal` carries no comment or remark noting that these claims are informational.

### .NET version

10.0.14, and the code is the same on release/8.0 and release/9.0.

### Anything else?

Happy to send a pull request if you want one, either making the Name claim consistent with the
DN claim or just documenting the difference, whichever you would prefer.

Issues.Title: Embedding components in MVC views and Razor Pages with Blazor Web App
Issues.Body:
MVC views and Razor Pages can render Razor components with the component tag helper and `Html.RenderComponentAsync`. This is currently supported only with the classic configuration:

- Server: `AddServerSideBlazor` + `MapBlazorHub` + `blazor.server.js`
- WebAssembly: `blazor.webassembly.js`

The server-side rendering is already shared with the Blazor Web App model. Since .NET 8, the tag helper uses the same renderer and emits the same component markers, and `blazor.web.js` can activate those components.

**Goal:** feature parity with the classic model using the Blazor Web App configuration (`AddRazorComponents` + `blazor.web.js`) for Interactive Server and Interactive WebAssembly, including both on the same page. This is a prerequisite for obsoleting the classic hosting APIs (#62761).

**Non-goals (follow-ups, further discussion):**
- Interactive Auto from the tag helper (#52522)
- Static SSR page features inside tag-helper components (forms handling, streaming rendering, `NotFound()`)

## Subproblems

- JS initializers: the server-rendered initializer list is not emitted on MVC pages, so newer initializer hooks silently never run, while classic hooks run only through a fallback.
- Interactive Server and WebAssembly endpoints can only be mapped through a root `App` component or the classic `MapBlazorHub`. The existing endpoint options and conventions must also be available without them.
- Misconfiguration (for example, a hub that isn't mapped) is only detected in the browser, not at render time.
- `<persist-component-state />` fails on pages with both Server and WebAssembly components. Antiforgery, authentication and culture state for WebAssembly components depend on it.
- Enhanced navigation must not run on MVC / Razor Pages pages. Today every link click or programmatic navigation executes the MVC action twice, and MVC error pages are merged into the current page (AspNetCore.Docs#34110).
- Server-sent `blazor.web.js` options are applied too late on initial load (main only). Needs a bug fix.
- Hosting setup must be verified and documented: script reference, import map, `<base href>`, projects without `.razor` files.
- There are no E2E tests for MVC / Razor Pages with `blazor.web.js`.
- The docs currently cover integration with the old model.

Issues.Title: Embedding components in JS apps with Blazor Web App
Issues.Body:
The classic scripts (`blazor.server.js`, `blazor.webassembly.js`) let JavaScript apps (React, Angular, plain JS) render Blazor components in two ways:
- JS root components (`RegisterForJavaScript` + `Blazor.rootComponents.add`)
- custom elements (`RegisterCustomElement`)

See [Use Razor components in JavaScript apps and SPA frameworks](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/components/js-spa-frameworks).

Neither works with the Blazor Web App model (`AddRazorComponents` + `blazor.web.js`). `blazor.web.js` starts a runtime only when the page contains server-rendered component markers, and a JavaScript app page has none. The docs currently point users to the classic scripts.

**Goal:** feature parity with the classic scripts using the Blazor Web App model, for Interactive Server or Interactive WebAssembly, one render mode per page. This is a prerequisite for obsoleting the classic hosting model (#62761).

**Non-goals (follow ups, further discussion):**
- Server and WebAssembly on the same page
- Interactive Auto
- Enhanced navigation on embedded pages
- Lazy runtime start
- Multiple Blazor apps per document (#38128)

## Subproblems

- Starting the Server circuit or the WebAssembly runtime on a page without server-rendered markers, so that `Blazor.rootComponents` is available after `Blazor.start()`.
- Selecting the render mode for the page, and failing clearly when a second render mode is used.
- Discovering and running JS initializers (including the CustomElements module) without the server-rendered initializer list.
- Making custom elements work with both render modes.
- Keeping `blazor.web.js` navigation behavior (enhanced navigation, focus handling, form validation) from interfering with the JavaScript app's router. This is shared with the MVC/Razor Pages issue.
- Server: keeping the circuit alive for the lifetime of the page, as the classic script does.
- Server: running `CircuitHandler`s for circuits that only host JS roots. This looks broken in `blazor.server.js` too (needs a repro).
- WebAssembly: starting the host when there is no initial set of server-rendered components.
- WebAssembly: providing the environment and browser configuration that a Web App normally sends through the server-rendered page.
- WebAssembly: making sure the existing ways to load fingerprinted framework assets without an import map keep working.
- WebAssembly: `[PersistentState]` in JS roots (suspected null reference, needs a repro).
- Hosting setup for projects without `.razor` files, `<base href>`, and JavaScript dev servers on another origin.
- E2E tests for both render modes, and restoring the Blazor Web App sections of the docs.

Issues.Title: MVC validation repeatedly traverses shared object graphs without any limit
Issues.Body:
MVC's `ValidationVisitor` detects cycles along the current recursion path, but revisits shared objects through every distinct path. For some shared-reference graphs, validation work therefore grows exponentially with the number of distinct objects.

This is reachable through JSON model binding when an application enables `ReferenceHandler.Preserve` and accepts a recursive DTO with validation rules. JSON `$id`/`$ref` metadata can represent these shared references compactly.

For example, consider a DTO with `Left` and `Right` child properties and a validation rule that succeeds:

```text
root.Left  = root.Right  = sharedChild
sharedChild.Left = sharedChild.Right = sharedLeaf
```

Although this graph contains only three distinct objects, the leaf is validated through four paths. Each additional shared branching level doubles the number of leaf visits.

`MaxValidationDepth` limits path depth, not total work. The model-error limit does not stop repeated validation when the rules succeed.

**Expected:** MVC provides a bound on aggregate validation work while preserving path-specific validation behavior.

**Actual:** Shared subgraphs are traversed repeatedly without an aggregate work limit, potentially causing disproportionate CPU use.

# Add `review-candidate-verifier` to `review-pull-request`

Adds a post-gate verification subagent (`review-candidate-verifier`) to the local `review-pull-request` skill so provisional findings are checked against the frozen diff and source, and surfaces `unresolved` and `discarded` candidates inline with the verifier/coordinator rationale so a human reviewer can make the final call.

## Description

Right now, `review-pull-request` sometimes publishes speculative findings as confirmed defects from the diff alone, such as assuming multi-threaded callers on single-threaded WebAssembly code (`#70106`, tracked in `#70235`) or unverified external MSAL initialization races (`#66055`).

An earlier draft of the verifier (`v4`) filtered out almost all of those false positives, but it had two drawbacks:
- It occasionally dropped a real regression (`V23` on `#69782`) by treating a new unit test added by the PR on a different layer as proof that the regression was "intended."
- When it demoted or discarded a candidate, that candidate was removed from `NEW_FINDINGS`, so it no longer surfaced inline at `file:line` for a human to see why it was disputed.

This PR (`v5`) adds the verifier with a stricter contract rule and inline confidence tiers (`verified`, `question`, `unresolved`, `discarded`) so nothing is silently lost:

1. **Runs a fresh `review-candidate-verifier` subagent on provisional `NEW_FINDINGS`** before the final review is emitted.
2. **Checks 4 required links for every candidate**:
   - **Changed line**: anchored to a right-side line touched by the PR.
   - **Trigger**: a realistic caller/input path reaches that line.
   - **Old vs. new**: the behavior actually changed compared to the base commit (not pre-existing).
   - **Effect**: the change causes a concrete regression or violates an existing contract.
3. **Fixes the "PR test as contract" blind spot**:

Issues.Title: Harden MapStaticAssets headers for authorization-gated endpoints
Issues.Body:
`MapStaticAssets()` replays the `Cache-Control` value stored in the build-time endpoints manifest for every asset (`StaticAssetsInvoker.ApplyResponseHeadersAsync`, `src/StaticAssets/src/StaticAssetsInvoker.cs`). For fingerprinted assets this is `max-age=31536000, immutable`. It is applied even when the endpoint requires authorization (`.RequireAuthorization()`, `[Authorize]` metadata or a fallback policy).

This is correct for public assets. For authorization-gated assets, the browser cache entry outlives the server-side access decision. After access is revoked, the asset can still be served from the local cache for up to a year without contacting the server, for example on a shared browser profile.

### Expected behavior

An endpoint that requires authorization should not emit `max-age=31536000, immutable`.

### Proposed fix

When the endpoint has authorization requirements, emit `Cache-Control: private, no-cache` instead. ETag revalidation still works, so authorization re-runs on each use and unchanged assets return 304.

Check `IAuthorizeData` without `IAllowAnonymous` in the endpoint metadata, after conventions have run, in `StaticAssetEndpointFactory.Create`. Fallback policies are not endpoint metadata, so they need either a per-request check or documentation.

### Alternatives

- Per-request check of the authenticated user (covers fallback policies, but adds hot-path cost).
- Private caching with a short `max-age` and no `immutable`.
- An opt-in convention to choose the cache policy per endpoint group.
- Documentation only: add a note to "Static file authorization".

Issues.Body:
# Add keyboard navigation and row activation to QuickGrid

Enable keyboard navigation and activation for clickable QuickGrid rows.

## Description

QuickGrid rows with `OnRowClick` currently respond to pointer clicks but are skipped by keyboard navigation. This change automatically exposes those tables as interactive grids and provides a single Tab entry point, arrow-key row/cell navigation, and Enter activation through the existing callback. Grids without `OnRowClick` retain ordinary table semantics.

Left and Right cycle through the cells and the whole row. Enter/F2 accesses controls inside a cell, Escape returns to the cell, and leaving the grid resets entry to its first visible data row. Home/End navigation, row selection, and Space activation are not added.

Virtualized navigation uses the existing `Virtualize.ScrollToItemAsync` path to load destinations outside the rendered window. Navigation follows current keyed-row positions after insertion and stops at real data rows rather than pagination padding.

Adds two browser regression tests using existing test components: keyboard activation with keyed insertion and visible reentry, and delayed virtualized data loading followed by activation of a newly loaded item. No sample changes or new test component are included.

This changes the default semantics and tab order of grids using `OnRowClick`, including how nested controls are reached. No public .NET signatures are added.

Fixes dotnet/aspnetcore-scenario-tests#157

Issues.Title: .NET 11 regression: malformed linker XML in Components.Endpoints causes IL2101 during trimmed publishing
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug

`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Endpoints` embeds an `ILLink.Substitutions.xml` resource whose assembly `fullname` incorrectly targets `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Forms`. This causes IL2101 during trimmed publishing.

This affects trimmed publishing of Blazor applications and can also occur in non-Blazor applications. A console application referencing `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App` and using `IHtmlHelper` reproduces the problem without RazorSlices, Razor files, MVC services, or Blazor registration.

When IL2101 is treated as an error, publishing fails with NETSDK1144.

### Expected Behavior

The embedded linker XML targets the correct assembly, and the application publishes without IL2101, as it does with .NET 10.

### Steps To Reproduce

Using .NET SDK `11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148`, create a console application with these files.

**Repro.csproj**
```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net11.0</TargetFramework>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <FrameworkReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.App" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

**Program.cs**
```csharp
System.Console.WriteLine(
    typeof(Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Rendering.IHtmlHelper).FullName);
```

Publish with trimming enabled:
```powershell
dotnet publish -c Release -r win-x64 --self-contained true -p:PublishAot=false -p:PublishTrimmed=true -p:ILLinkTreatWarningsAsErrors=false
```

Observe IL2101 for the embedded `ILLink.Substitutions.xml` resource in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Endpoints`.

Repeat with `-p:ILLinkTreatWarningsAsErrors=true` to observe publishing fail with NETSDK1144.

### Exceptions (if any)

IL2101 reports malformed linker XML. Treating the warning as an error causes NETSDK1144.

### .NET Version

Reported with SDK `11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148`.

The equivalent `net10.0` reproduction using SDK `10.0.403` and runtime/linker packs `10.0.14` does not emit IL2101.

### Anything else?

According to Damian's investigation:

- ViewFeatures leads the linker to Components.Endpoints. Its XML is parsed even though Endpoints is unmarked and removed from the final output.
- The malformed resource was introduced by commit `309d909185` in #65903 and remained incorrect on the inspected `main` snapshot.
- The .NET 10 linker already performs the cross-assembly XML check, so this is a framework resource regression rather than a new linker diagnostic.

This issue isolates the IL2101 problem described in #69270 and tracks its impact on both Blazor and non-Blazor applications.

**Proposed servicing target:** the first .NET 11 servicing window in December, subject to servicing approval.

# Reuse RenderBatchWriter across render batches in RemoteRenderer

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (Follow-up to review feedback on #70125.)

Stop allocating a new batch writer and stream for every Blazor Server render batch.

## Description

Follow-up to @pavelsavara's suggestion on #70125. `RemoteRenderer.UpdateDisplayAsync` created a new `ArrayBuilderMemoryStream`, `RenderBatchWriter`, `BinaryWriter`, string `ArrayBuilder` and dedup `Dictionary` for every render batch. This PR keeps one writer per renderer and points its stream at each batch's own output buffer.

On the real `RemoteRenderer.UpdateDisplayAsync` + ack path, this halves allocations for a small interactive update (776 → 392 B) and cuts time by about 8%.

**Why this is safe**
- Each batch still gets its own `ArrayBuilder<byte>` output buffer. That buffer is kept in the unacknowledged-batch queue until the client acks it, so it is never shared or reused.
- `UpdateDisplayAsync` runs on the renderer's dispatcher, and `Renderer` guards it with `_isBatchInProgress`, so a renderer never writes two batches at once. The writer belongs to one renderer, so nothing is shared across circuits.
- `RenderBatchWriter.Write` now resets its string table in a `finally`, including when a write throws. Between batches the writer holds no strings, and its string `ArrayBuilder` has returned its array to the pool. So the renderer never needs to dispose it, and a dispose racing a render can't return a buffer that is still in use.
- If a batch used more than 128 deduplicated strings, the dictionary is replaced instead of cleared, so one large render doesn't leave a big table alive for the rest of the circuit.
- The wire format and the WebAssembly/WebView callers are unchanged, and there are no public API changes.

**Tests:** two new `RenderBatchWriterTest` cases reuse one writer for two batches, one of them after a failed write. Both fail on `main`, where the second batch's string table still holds the first batch's strings, and pass here. Server (396), WebView (16) and WebAssembly (56) unit tests pass locally.

### Benchmark

BenchmarkDotNet, in-process. The benchmark drives the real path: `RemoteRenderer.UpdateDisplayAsync(batch)` followed by `OnRenderCompletedAsync(batchId)`, with an offline client so no SignalR send. The batches are the same as in #70125's `RenderBatchWriterBenchmark` (a 5-edit counter-style update, and a 200-row table initial render). I ran 3 interleaved rounds (main, PR, main, PR, main, PR) on a 2-core Linux VM.

| Method | main R1 / R2 / R3 | PR R1 / R2 / R3 | Δ time | Allocated main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small batch | 829.6 / 864.6 / 819.8 ns | 778.2 / 792.1 / 750.5 ns | **−7.7%** | **776 B → 392 B (−49%)** |
| Large batch | 97.9 / 96.4 / 96.4 µs | 93.6 / 94.8 / 93.4 µs | **−3.1%** | **5,032 B → 4,401 B (−13%)** |

<details><summary>Benchmark harness (throwaway; not part of this PR)</summary>

A console project inside the repo with `AssemblyName=Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.Tests` (for internals access), referencing Server and SignalR.Core, and using `InProcessEmitToolchain` + `MemoryDiagnoser`:

```csharp
[GlobalSetup] // options = new CircuitOptions(); jsRuntime = new RemoteJSRuntime(...); services registers IJSRuntime
_renderer = new BenchRenderer(services, options, jsRuntime); // RemoteRenderer subclass, offline CircuitClientProxy
_nextBatchId = 2; // RemoteRenderer pre-increments _nextRenderId = 1

private Task RenderAndAck(in RenderBatch batch)
{
    var task = _renderer.Update(in batch);              // => UpdateDisplayAsync(in batch)
    _renderer.OnRenderCompletedAsync(_nextBatchId++, null); // dequeues + disposes the batch buffer
    if (!task.IsCompleted) { throw new InvalidOperationException("Batch was not acknowledged."); }
    return task;
}
```
</details>

This is independent of #70125 (which changes how frames and edits are encoded); both touch `RenderBatchWriter.cs` but in different methods.

### Follow-up: `IpcSender` (WebView) and `WebAssemblyRenderer` (7e0ca8700a)

At reviewer request, the same reuse is applied to the other two `RenderBatchWriter` call sites:

- **`IpcSender.ApplyRenderBatch`** (WebView): the writer and stream are cached in a private field. Each batch takes them with `Interlocked.Exchange` and puts them back in `finally`, so two concurrent callers can never share them; if the cache is empty, a new writer is created. The per-batch `ArrayBuilder<byte>` is now also disposed (returned to the pool) in `finally`, once the base64 message string has copied its contents. On `main` it was never disposed.
- **`WebAssemblyRenderer.UpdateDisplayOutOfProcess`**: the writer and stream are cached in fields (the renderer is single-threaded) and retargeted at each batch's own `ArrayBuilder`. The existing `finally { arrayBuilder.Dispose(); }` is unchanged.

**WebView `IpcSender.ApplyRenderBatch`**: real path. BenchmarkDotNet, 3 interleaved rounds, mean of each round:

| Batch | main R1/R2/R3 | PR R1/R2/R3 | Allocated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small | 1.860* / 1.252 / 1.288 µs | 1.048 / 1.041 / 1.061 µs | 5 KB → 3 KB |
| Large | 438.2 / 404.1 / 412.5 µs | 420.8 / 424.1 / 396.6 µs (noise) | 509 KB → 445 KB |

\*R1 main small had high variance (median 1.273 µs).

**WebAssembly out-of-process sequence**: the real `UpdateDisplayOutOfProcess` needs browser JS interop, so this benchmark reproduces its exact serialize + `ToArray` steps (UTF-16 string table) on CoreCLR, main pattern vs PR pattern:

| Batch | main R1/R2/R3 | PR R1/R2/R3 | Allocated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small | 567.4 / 558.7 / 552.0 ns | 490.5 / 496.8 / 485.1 ns (−12%) | 880 B → 496 B |
| Large | 102.6 / 101.7 / 102.7 µs | 99.4 / 120.3* / 99.0 µs (noise) | 70,457 B → 69,825 B |

\*outlier round.

Tests: Components.Server 396, Components.WebView 16 and Components.WebAssembly 56 all pass.

Issues.Title: Use End in the variable-height table test
Issues.Body:
Replace the pixel jump with one End key press.

## Description

This test was added in #64964. Recently there can be seen multiple failures connected with this test https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_test/analytics?definitionId=87&contextType=build. The triggering change is not known but it can happen randomly when loaded variable items are much bigger towards the end of the list than these at the start of the list.

The old `window.scrollTo` used the table's current estimated height. Because the variable height items were not rendered yet at the time of the scroll, the viewport was bouncing back once they loaded from placeholders. As a result, the viewport was not always at the very end of the list and the bottom spacer was not visible for inspection. 

The test now sends **End** key stroke - End/Home are programmed in such a way that they always land at the requested position, without bouncing back.

**Local failure rates:**

Issues.Title: Kestrel HTTP/2 performs only two of the four field validations RFC 9113 8.2.1 requires: a space or a colon in a header name, and leading or trailing whitespace in a value, are accepted
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

I searched open and closed issues here for HTTP/2 header name validation, field name tokens, colons in header names, and leading or trailing whitespace in field values, and did not find this reported. The nearest one I found is #69574, which is about the connection-specific header list rather than field name and field value characters.

### Describe the bug

RFC 9113 §8.2.1 lists four minimal validations an HTTP/2 implementation MUST perform on field names and values. Kestrel performs two of them and not the other two.

It rejects uppercase field names, and it rejects NUL, LF and CR inside a field value. It accepts:

* a field name containing an ASCII space, which §8.2.1 forbids as part of the range 0x00-0x20,
* a field name containing a colon,
* a field value that starts or ends with an ASCII space.

The spec's wording on the last two:

> With the exception of pseudo-header fields (Section 8.3), which have a name that starts with a single colon, field names MUST NOT include a colon (ASCII COLON, 0x3a).

> A field value MUST NOT start or end with an ASCII whitespace character (ASCII SP or HTAB, 0x20 or 0x09).

and the consequence it attaches to all four bullets:

> A request or response that contains a field that violates any of these conditions MUST be treated as malformed (Section 8.1.1).

The same section says why the colon is on that list:

> Failure to validate fields can be exploited for request smuggling attacks. In particular, unvalidated fields might enable attacks when messages are forwarded using HTTP/1.1 [HTTP/1.1], where characters such as carriage return (CR), line feed (LF), and COLON are used as delimiters.

CR and LF are the two that Kestrel does reject. COLON is in the same sentence and is accepted.

### Measured behaviour

A minimal app whose handler reports the header name and value it was handed, byte for byte, with Kestrel listening for HTTP/1.1 on one loopback port and HTTP/2 cleartext on another. The HTTP/2 requests come from a raw client using HPACK literal-never-indexed with no Huffman coding, so the bytes on the wire are exactly the bytes in the table.

| what the client sends | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x-probe: AB` (control) | name `x-probe`, value `AB` | name `x-probe`, value `AB` |
| `x:probe: AB` | name `x`, value `probe: AB` | name `x:probe`, value `AB` |
| `x probe: AB` | **400 Bad Request** | name `x probe`, value `AB` |
| `x-probe:  AB` (extra leading space) | value `AB` | value ` AB` |
| `x-probe: AB ` (trailing space) | value `AB` | value `AB ` |

The control agrees on both protocols, so the two paths are being measured consistently. The three HTTP/2 rows are identical on 10.0.14 and on 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148, so this is not something the .NET 11 work already covered.

The `x:probe` row is the smuggling shape the spec describes, demonstrated inside one server: those bytes mean a header named `x` with the value `probe: AB` to Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser, and a header named `x:probe` with the value `AB` to its HTTP/2 parser.

### Where it comes from

`Http2Connection.ValidateHeaderContent` checks the name for uppercase letters and nothing else:

```csharp
private void ValidateHeaderContent(ReadOnlySpan<byte> name, ReadOnlySpan<byte> value)
{
    // A request or response containing uppercase header field names MUST be treated as malformed
    for (var i = 0; i < name.Length; i++)
    {
        if (((uint)name[i] - 65) <= (90 - 65))
        {
            ...
        }
    }
}
```

§8.2.1 carries a note that explains how this came to be the only check:

> Note: An implementation that validates fields according to the definitions in Sections 5.1 and 5.5 of [HTTP] only needs an additional check that field names do not include uppercase characters.

The uppercase check is that additional check. What is missing is the base validation it is meant to be added to.

`Http3Stream.ValidateHeaderContent` has the same shape, so I expect HTTP/3 to behave the same way, but I measured HTTP/2 only and would rather not claim HTTP/3 without measuring it.

### Why it matters, and what it is not

Kestrel as the origin server does not misframe anything here. The body comes from DATA frames, and I measured no framing divergence.

What does change is what the application is handed. Code that compares a header value as a string sees `" AB"` over HTTP/2 where it sees `"AB"` over HTTP/1.1, from identical client bytes. Code that forwards the request to an HTTP/1.1 hop has to re-serialize a name that is not a token, and `x:probe: AB` on an HTTP/1.1 request becomes a different header with a different value, as the table above shows Kestrel's own HTTP/1.1 parser doing.

I am not reporting a remotely exploitable vulnerability in Kestrel itself. I am reporting that two of the four MUST validations in §8.2.1 are absent, that one of the two missing ones is the character the spec singles out for smuggling when messages are forwarded over HTTP/1.1, and that the result is a protocol-dependent view of the same header.

### Expected behaviour

A field name containing a space or a colon, and a field value starting or ending with a space, are treated as malformed on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, the same way an uppercase field name already is and the same way Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 path already rejects a name that is not a token.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run an app with Kestrel listening with `HttpProtocols.Http1` on one loopback port and `HttpProtocols.Http2` on another, whose handler writes `Request.Headers` out as hex so a changed value cannot look like an unchanged one.
2. Send `GET /x HTTP/1.1` with the header line `x probe: AB` to the HTTP/1.1 port. It answers 400 Bad Request.
3. Send the same name and value over HTTP/2 to the other port, as an HPACK literal-never-indexed field with no Huffman coding. It answers 200 and the application sees a header named `x probe`.
4. Repeat with the name `x:probe`, and with a value that has a leading or a trailing space, comparing the two ports each time.

### Exceptions (if any)

_No response_

### .NET Version

10.0.14 and 11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148, Linux x86_64

### Anything else?

Both rows of the table were taken on both runtimes. The HTTP/2 behaviour did not differ between them.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "Kestrel HTTP/2 performs only two of the four field validations RFC 9113 8.2.1 requires: a space or a colon in a header name, and leading or trailing whitespace in a value, are accepted" (#70237)

Issues.Title: [Review agent] False positive: unsupported-concurrency race in AuthorizationMessageHandler on #70106
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

The hosted `/review` agent published a P2 concurrency finding on [#70106](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#discussion_r4431751648). It claimed that `NotifyAuthenticationStateChanged`, raised on another thread, can interleave between the cancellation check and the cache write in `AuthorizationMessageHandler.SendAsync` and cache a stale token.

At the reviewed head, the check and both cache writes are synchronous: no `await` falls between them. Blazor WebAssembly runs single-threaded, so the claimed interleaving requires multithreaded execution that is not a supported configuration. The finding was later withdrawn on the PR. This tracks a **review-agent failure**, not an authentication product bug.

- Hosted run: [41202500880](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/41202500880).
- Reviewed head: `2edf3761692afe15475075eb2fc0088566162045`.
- Reviewer/guidance revision: `4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5`; observed model: `gpt-5.6-sol`.
- Verdict: **Wrong for supported configurations**. The race is reachable only under unsupported multithreaded execution.

### Expected Behavior

A race finding should be accepted only after it identifies a supported caller or producer that actually schedules both operations concurrently. That a host or runtime is capable of threading shows the code can be reached, not that the two operations overlap.

The two routed guide workers disagreed here: Cross-Cutting reported the candidate and Blazor Components reported nothing. The coordinator resolved the disagreement by accepting the candidate. When re-checking does not settle the trigger and causal path, the skill already requires recording the candidate as `UNRESOLVED` ([SKILL.md:213-215](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/4f556f73a610b386e5ec29355a300e493d30c4c5/.github/skills/review-pull-request/SKILL.md#L213-L215)).

### Steps To Reproduce

This is reproducible from the retained review and immutable source; no new reviewer dispatch is needed.

1. Read the [published finding](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#discussion_r4431751648) and the [review summary](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#pullrequestreview-5722771822), which records the worker disagreement.
2. At the reviewed head, inspect [AuthorizationMessageHandler.cs:71-81](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/2edf3761692afe15475075eb2fc0088566162045/src/Components/WebAssembly/WebAssembly.Authentication/src/Services/AuthorizationMessageHandler.cs#L71-L81). The only interleaving points are the `RequestAccessToken` awaits, which the authentication-state `CancellationTokenSource` already covers. The check at line 77 and the writes at lines 79-80 run without yielding.
3. See the [author reply](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#discussion_r4431799752) and the [follow-up review](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70106#pullrequestreview-5723402763). The ordering reproduced only under genuinely multithreaded execution, which current Blazor WebAssembly does not support, so the finding was withdrawn.

### Exceptions (if any)

None. The published repro needs a second thread to run the callback while the handler is paused between two synchronous statements. That cannot happen on the supported single-threaded runtime.

### .NET Version

N/A for reproducing this reviewer failure from saved output and source.

### Anything else?

Parent tracking epic: [#70231](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/70231).

Exploratory evidence from one published finding; this does not estimate general reviewer accuracy. In offline replays of this same claim, reviewers repeatedly justified acceptance by "the host supports multithreading" rather than by a concrete concurrent producer. Candidate skill changes for this pattern are being evaluated locally, with real-race sentinels to avoid suppressing valid concurrency findings.

Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?" (#2056)

Issues.Body:
My security team escalated to me that the `PasswordHasher` is vulnerable to heap inspection, as the password is of type `String`. 
It should be instead a byte array / span of bytes cleared at the end of the process, as it is done by any cryptographic operation in corefx. CC @bartonjs.
Same problem with any password related types (`IPasswordValidator`, and maybe also the `IUserPasswordStore`)

Issues.Body:
Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

These are my main concerns:

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

I used to be able to use `dotnet watch` in Visual Studio by adding the following section to `launchSettings.json` and starting the project without debugging using CTRL + F5.

```
    "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },
```

This used to work in ASP.NET Core 1.1 but no longer does. According to https://github.com/aspnet/DotNetTools/issues/404 the new format for ASP.NET Core 2.0 is:

```
   "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "workingDirectory": "C:\\Users\\namc\\source\\repos\\WebApplication2\\WebApplication2",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
```

The problem with this is the hard coded `executablePath` which is Windows specific and the `workingDirectory` which is specific to wherever I did a Git clone on my local machine.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Token-based antiforgery and automatic cross-origin CSRF protection now record a shared verdict through `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.

Validating again inside the Blazor SSR endpoint duplicated work and could produce a result different from the middleware verdict. Generating tokens without token-based antiforgery middleware also produced tokens that nothing validated.

### Recommended action

If your Blazor SSR app relies on antiforgery tokens for form validation or rendering, ensure that it calls `app.UseAntiforgery()`:
```csharp
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAntiforgery();
```

# ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach end of support on April 13, 2027

> Update: The ASP.NET Core 2.3 end of support date was updated from April 7, 2027 to April 13, 2027 to align with the Microsoft servicing release cycles.

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

This announcement provides the required 12 months of advance notice, as defined by the [Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/faq/general-lifecycle#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-tools-) for products classified as "Tools."

## Current support policy

ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages (latest patched version only) are currently [supported](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/aspnet#dotnet-core) on .NET Framework, following the support cycle for those .NET Framework versions. After April 13, 2027, this support will end regardless of the .NET Framework version in use.

Note that the [ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/aspnet/2.3-packages) include the Entity Framework 2.3 packages, which will end support on the same date.

## Impact of end of support

After ASP.NET Core 2.3 reaches end of support:

- No new security updates will be issued for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- Continuing to use an unsupported version may expose your applications to security vulnerabilities.
- Technical support will no longer be available for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- The ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages will be deprecated.

## Upgrade recommendation

We recommend upgrading to a [currently supported version of .NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet), such as .NET 10 (LTS).

To help with the upgrade process, we recommend using [GitHub Copilot modernization](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/porting/github-copilot-app-modernization/overview), which provides AI-powered assistance to help you analyze, plan, and execute your migration to a modern .NET version.

Issues.Body:
Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

## Implementation

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

- Triggers on `issues.opened` and `issues.labeled` events with "Breaking change" label
- Creates issue in docs repo with:
  - Title: `[Breaking Change] <original title>`
  - Body: Link to source issue, full context
  - Labels: `breaking-change`, `aspnet/Announcements`
- Posts comment on source issue with link to docs issue

## Duplicate Prevention

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating
- Concurrency control keyed on issue number

## Error Handling

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search
- Search failures → proceed with creation (fail open to avoid missing docs)
- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

## Setup Required

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Deprecating WebHostBuilder,  IWebHost, and WebHost
Issues.Body:
### Description

`WebHostBuilder` was replaced by `HostBuilder` ([generic host](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder)) in 3.0 and we also added [`WebApplicationBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) in 6.0.

We are now marking `WebHostBuilder` as obsolete to encourage users to move on to the alternatives which is where future investments will occur, and we're also marking `IWebHost` and `WebHost` as deprecated to clean up other parts of the now obsolete web host story.

### Version

.NET 10 RC 1

### Previous behavior

```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

### New behavior

Using `WebHostBuilder` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR004**:
> warning ASPDEPR004: WebHostBuilder is deprecated in favor of HostBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/004.

Using `IWebHost` or `WebHost` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR008**:
> warning ASPDEPR008: WebHost is obsolete. Use HostBuilder or WebApplicationBuilder instead. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/008.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [x] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [ ] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

We recommend the use of `HostBuilder` and `WebApplication` going forward over `WebHostBuilder` because they have all the features of `WebHostBuilder` and will be the focus of future investment.

### Recommended action

See https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/generic-host or https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/webapplication for more details on the different hosting models. As well as [HostBuilder replaces WebHostBuilder](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder) and [Introducing WebApplication](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) for migration guides.

Below is an example of converting `WebHostBuilder` to `HostBuilder`:

**Before**
```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

**After**
```csharp
using var host = new HostBuilder()
    .ConfigureWebHost(webHostBuilder =>
    {
        webHostBuilder
            .UseTestServer() // If using TestServer
            .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
            .UseStartup()
            .UseKestrel();
    })
    .Build();
await host.StartAsync();

var testServer = host.GetTestServer();
```

Both Copilot and ChatGpt have given good results so far when asked to convert a WebHostBuilder example to use HostBuilder. Below is an example prompt:
<details>
<summary>Example AI Prompt</summary>

> Can you convert
>
> var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
>     .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
>     .UseStartup()
>     .UseKestrel();
> // Test code might use TestServer:
> var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
>
> to use HostBuilder.

</details>

### Affected APIs

`public class Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.WebHostBuilder`
`public interface Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.IWebHost`
`public static class Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebHost`

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/63480

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Exception diagnostics are suppressed when `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns true
Issues.Body:
### Description

The [ASP.NET Core exception handler middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#exception-handler-page), `UseExceptionHandler()`, is responsible for catching and processing unhandled exceptions from ASP.NET Core requests.

In .NET 8, we introduced [`IExceptionHandler`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#iexceptionhandler). Implementations of `IExceptionHandler` are registered with dependency injection and invoked by the middleware. An implementation can return `true` from `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` to indicate that the exception has been handled. The middleware stops processing the exception once it has been handled.

In .NET 10, we're changing the default behavior so that the middleware no longer records diagnostics for exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

### Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

### Previous behavior

The exception handler middleware recorded diagnostics about exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

The exception diagnostics are:

- Logging `UnhandledException` to `ILogger`.
- Writing the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HandledException` event to `EventSource`.
- Adding the `error.type` tag to the `http.server.request.duration` metric.

### New behavior

If `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns `true`, then exception diagnostics are no longer recorded by default.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

ASP.NET Core users have given feedback that the previous behavior was undesirable. Their `IExceptionHandler` implementation reported that the exception was handled, but the error handling middleware still recorded the error in the app's telemetry.

We are changing ASP.NET Core to follow the behavior expected by users by suppressing diagnostics when `IExceptionHandler` handles the exception. We're also adding configuration options to customize exception diagnostics behavior if needed.

### Recommended action

If you want handled exceptions to continue recording telemetry, you can use the new `ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` option:

```cs
app.UseExceptionHandler(new ExceptionHandlerOptions
{
    SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = context => false;
});
```

The context passed to the callback includes information about the exception, the request, and whether the exception was handled. Returning `false` from the callback indicates that diagnostics shouldn't be suppressed. This restores the previous behavior.

### References

- Issue: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54554
- PR: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/59074

### Affected APIs

- `UseExceptionHandler()`
- `IExceptionHandler`
